name: Professional Networking

claims.claim_text: Being able to telephone someone and describe a problem is a working technical capability, not a social nicety. Trying to derive everything from books alone is hopeless, and the engineers who lack the habit of making and keeping a hundred acquaintances are handicapped in solving problems, not just in advancing.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got to be able to call somebody up and go, hey, you know, this is happening
claims.speaker: Howard Johnson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Howard Johnson - Winsome Waveform Wizardry

claims.claim_text: Telling an engineer to network is useless advice because it names an outcome rather than an action. The version that transfers is narrower: talk technical. Engineers who cannot make small talk can usually discuss a circuit indefinitely, and that conversation produces the same relationships.
claims.quote_verbatim: remember people telling me to network and I'd be like, screw you, I don't know what that means
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: When someone asks who does a particular kind of work, the names that come up first are the people the recommender actually cares about — and that ordering is formed in person, over dinner or a handshake, rather than through online interaction. This is the concrete mechanism by which relationships convert into work.
claims.quote_verbatim: the ones that i give a crap about i'm going to call first
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: We're Sorry! But Apple Ain't! - Remorseless RAM Racketeering

claims.claim_text: An introvert does not have to become an extrovert to benefit from this. Being outward for a day or two and then retreating to recover is a workable pattern, and it produces the same in-person connections that carry more weight than remote ones.
claims.quote_verbatim: i can do it for a day or two days and then i go back into my cave
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: We're Sorry! But Apple Ain't! - Remorseless RAM Racketeering

claims.claim_text: Successive jobs come through people already known — a former colleague from an internship, a field applications engineer who mentions an opening. The mechanism is unglamorous and specific: the occasional catch-up message and the offer of a coffee are what keep those channels open.
claims.quote_verbatim: got my, my next jobs because I knew people
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The stronger position is the inverse of the usual advice: rather than knowing people, be known. Someone with a public reputation announces availability and is approached, instead of approaching others — which is a slower thing to build and a far more durable one.
claims.quote_verbatim: you knowing people, but people knowing you
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Publishing work substitutes for sociability. A repository, a blog, or documented projects make you findable without requiring the conversations, which matters because a substantial fraction of good engineers will not do the conversations.
claims.quote_verbatim: get known by putting your stuff out there if you're not a people person
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Connections matter most exactly where a candidate has least to show: the first couple of positions are the hardest to obtain and the ones where knowing someone changes the outcome most.
claims.quote_verbatim: when it's more early jobs, that's like the high value ones, the hard ones to get the first couple jobs
claims.speaker: Dave Young

claims.claim_text: The most effective route into a company is somebody technical on the inside who will smooth the way — and the modern precondition for having such a person is being visible online, so that they have something to point at when they vouch for you.
claims.quote_verbatim: your best bet is to have somebody on the inside that is technical
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: Moving from one kind of engineering to another needs demonstrable work: commit to a substantial project, budget real money and months for it, and finish it even if the result is pointless in itself. Nobody moves from test into design on an assertion of interest.
claims.quote_verbatim: would find a project, a meaty project, and make a commitment to it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The way to approach a design engineer is not to ask about design engineering. Take one of their products apart, bring the schematic with something circled, and ask why they did it that way rather than another — engineers will talk for hours about their own decisions, and the relationship forms out of the technical conversation.
claims.quote_verbatim: take one of the products that they've designed, right? Take it apart
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Buying people lunch is a concrete and unusually effective version of the advice: an hour of someone's time in exchange for a meal, spent asking about their work, is a low-cost way to learn what a role actually involves and to be remembered by the person doing it.
claims.quote_verbatim: her career turned when she started buying people lunch
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Talking to someone who holds the job you want is worthwhile even when that job will never open. What you take away is the skill set to develop and the shape the work actually has, which then gives a personal project something specific to aim at.
claims.quote_verbatim: understanding their background, understanding their daily work, understanding their skill set
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Standing out positively is worth deliberate effort, because being one more indistinguishable person in a crowd of four hundred means not being remembered when a hiring decision is made months later. The specific means matters less than being distinguishable at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: standing out in a positive way
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - The Ternary Tussle

claims.claim_text: Publishing work is the beginning rather than the end. Maintaining the relationships that follow pays off in ways that are hard to predict — the contact who has no job to offer still hears about jobs, and that indirect route is how most opportunities travel.
claims.quote_verbatim: past just publishing, you got to kind of maintain relationships
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: 555 Contest, Computer Museum, Octopart - The Green Pen Hornswoggle

claims.claim_text: Conference attendance is worth paying for personally and taking leave for, on the understanding that the value is meeting people rather than the talks. Walking the floor and talking to people is the activity; the programme is the excuse.
claims.quote_verbatim: always done it on my own dime. I've usually taken time off because I do it for networking
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: FPGAs, Robots & Thermocouples - Wampum's Wavering Worth

claims.claim_text: Small recurring domain-specific gatherings — an annual dinner for a particular speciality — put you in front of people who have been in that field for decades, which no general industry event and no online forum reproduces.
claims.quote_verbatim: a good chance to go and meet people interested in Analog and people that have been in the industry a long time
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Questioning Everyday Prototyping - Verrucose Vehicle Vitilitigation

claims.claim_text: A cold approach works when it is honest about itself: say how you found them, be specific about what interests you in their work, and make the interest genuine rather than flattering. Interest in the person is what gets the message read, which is the hardest part.
claims.quote_verbatim: be upfront, right? Like, hey, I found your email
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Lead with what you can offer, even if it is only an outside technical perspective on what they are building. There may be nothing you can give someone further along than you, in which case their own curiosity is the offer — but check for the real one first.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have something to offer in return, right, that's always good to lead with
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Anyone with a public profile receives more mail than they can answer, so brevity is the whole game and someone that prominent is the wrong first target. Approach people two steps ahead of you rather than twenty.
claims.quote_verbatim: Don't waffle
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The professional social network functions more as a directory than as a place relationships form. It is useful for being findable and for confirming who someone is; the searches run against it by recruiters are frequently so crude that the contact they generate is noise.
claims.quote_verbatim: more like a directory now
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A shared workspace is valuable precisely when you have no network and are trying to enter a field. Once you have your own industry contacts it adds little, and the people around you are likely to be in trades with no bearing on yours.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't have any networking already and you're looking to get into the field
claims.speaker: Scott Williams
claims.episode_title: Design & Manufacturing Consulting with Scott Williams from Xentronics

claims.claim_text: A consulting practice is generally built on the network that preceded it — the earlier colleagues who passed on opportunities and tip-offs — which means the groundwork has to be laid years before there is any intention of going independent.
claims.quote_verbatim: wouldn't be here without my network and who I've been working with
claims.speaker: Scott Williams
claims.episode_title: Design & Manufacturing Consulting with Scott Williams from Xentronics

claims.claim_text: Finding consulting clients started with attending entrepreneurship meetups in a new city and listening to what people were trying to build, looking for something worth helping with. Framing it as meeting people in a new place rather than as selling is what made it sustainable to keep doing.
claims.quote_verbatim: just started going to startup meetups, like entrepreneurship meetups
claims.speaker: Dave Young

claims.claim_text: Nontraditional careers in this field share a pattern rather than a credential: networking into jobs, finding mentors, and eventually working independently. Where a conventional route is closed, making the job is the remaining option, and it is a well-trodden one.
claims.quote_verbatim: she networked to jobs. She found mentors
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Hamvention, Arduino and Intel - Burdensome Background Battology

claims.claim_text: Remote study at a fraction of the cost gives up the in-person contact, the incidental relationships and the exposure to research method that constitute much of what a graduate degree is actually worth — which may still be the right trade for someone already inclined to work alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: you lose out on, you know, in-person contact, networking
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Hamvention, Arduino and Intel - Burdensome Background Battology

claims.claim_text: Electronics is a small industry and people circulate through it repeatedly — working alongside the same colleagues at three different companies over a career is unremarkable. That recurrence is what makes a reputation, good or bad, follow someone.
claims.quote_verbatim: the industry is so incestuous
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Documentation Is A Waste Of Time

claims.claim_text: Professional bodies are useful to independents in an unglamorous way: finding an accountant or the other auxiliary services a consultancy needs, from other members who have already solved the same problem.
claims.quote_verbatim: just finding accountants or finding similar types of services, like auxiliary services for consultants
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

attribution_notes: attribution_reliable was not trusted. ep624 (Scott Williams), ep232 (Dave Vandenbout), ep305 (Dave Young), ep35 (Jeri Ellsworth) and ep77 (Howard Johnson) label host questions with the guest's name; only material unambiguously the guest's own was used.

ep288 is a call-in episode where both hosts and the caller speak in a single long passage; claims are assigned by content, with the approach-a-design-engineer advice attributed to Dave Jones and the lunch and skill-set observations to Chris Gammell.
The observation attributed to Chris Gammell about buying people lunch is his relaying of Elecia White's account; it is kept as a reported practice rather than as his own experience.
Discussion of specific job markets, salaries and individual employers was excluded as neither transferable nor durable.
